title: India's Restaurant Sector Bets on Niche Cuisines Over Generic Menus
excerpt: Travellers returning with specific tastes, a food services market heading past $125 billion by 2030, and diners ordering 20% more unique cuisines are pushing Indian restaurants toward sharp, single-cuisine concepts.
body:
• India's restaurant sector is shifting from broad multi-cuisine menus to sharp, cuisine-specific niche concepts on high streets and in local markets, CYK Hospitalities director Pulkit Arora told FNB News.
  • The market backdrop is large: Swiggy and Kearney put India's food services market at $78 billion in 2025, rising to over $125 billion by 2030.
  • Experimentation is measurable — unique cuisines ordered per customer rose 20%, and hyper-regional Indian cuisines such as Goan, Bihari and Pahari are growing 2 to 8 times mainstream rates.
  • For diaspora readers and would-be restaurateurs: the winning formula is a specific regional or global niche, engineered margins from day one, and separate menus for dine-in and delivery.

India's restaurant industry is poised for a niche culinary revolution, according to Pulkit Arora, director of CYK Hospitalities, in an interview with FNB News. As Indians travel abroad at much higher rates and encounter regional cuisines and different forms of dining, Arora argues, they return wanting the same specificity at home — and the domestic market still lacks enough cuisine-specific restaurants on high streets and in local markets.

Beyond the Generic Menu

Arora's case is that success no longer lies in traditional menu staples. It requires sharp concepts, unique products and well-researched business models that prize consistency over chasing trends. That means a restaurant built around one cuisine, one format or one occasion — not a long menu trying to please everyone in a food court.

The demand data supports a move toward specificity. The Swiggy and Kearney 'How India Eats' report, reported by Bizz Buzz, found experimentation rising sharply: unique cuisines ordered per customer grew 20% and restaurants ordered from per customer grew 30%. Hyper-regional Indian cuisines — Goan, Bihari and Pahari among them — are growing at 2 to 8 times mainstream cuisines, while Korean, Vietnamese and Mexican food are becoming mainstream at growth indices of 17 times, 6 times and 3.7 times respectively.

A $125 Billion Backdrop

The niche shift is happening inside a rapidly expanding market. Swiggy and Kearney estimated India's food services market at $49 billion in 2019 and $78 billion in 2025, and projected it to cross $125 billion by 2030, with the organised segment driving over 60% of growth and overtaking the unorganised segment. Food services contribute 1.9% of India's GDP, against 5% in China and 6% in Brazil — headroom the report expects rising incomes and digital adoption to fill.

Dining-out growth beyond the top eight cities is running at twice the rate of those metros, the report added, and Gen Z dining-out is growing at three times other cohorts. In other words, the niche revolution is not only a Mumbai and Delhi story; smaller-city diners are experimenting too.

Discipline Behind the Concept

Arora pairs the creative argument with an operational one. Profitability, he argues, must be engineered at the concept stage, not rescued later — through recipe standardisation, yield analysis and vendor benchmarking. He warns against judging food cost by ingredient purchase price alone, without wastage, portioning, storage and inventory.

Technology, in his account, is now foundational infrastructure: point-of-sale systems, inventory management and recipe costing. But he cautions against over-automation, arguing that technology improves intelligence and efficiency while understanding people and managing experience remain human work. He also advises brands to separate dine-in and delivery, with channel-specific menus, because delivery customers buy convenience while dine-in customers buy atmosphere and interaction.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs who eat in India on visits — and for diaspora restaurateurs watching home trends — the direction is clear. Expect fewer generic 'multi-cuisine' restaurants and more single-idea rooms: a Goan kitchen, a Bihari table, a Korean counter, a dessert parlour with one perfected product. CYK Hospitalities itself is expanding into western and southern India, with resources allocated to Mumbai, and into central kitchens and food production consulting, FNB News reported.

Arora's final test for operators is substance over decoration: an experiential concept, he says, must connect the food, service format, architecture, music and story of the brand. A beautiful room earns a first visit. Only good food and hospitality earn the second.
